introduction-the-pray-and-deploy-era.core: Traditional network changes are typed into CLIs during maintenance windows, checked by eye, and validated by 'did anything break?'. Most outages are self-inflicted by such changes. NetDevOps and network verification bring software practices: configs in Git, automated testing, and mathematical analysis that proves properties such as reachability or isolation before a change is deployed.

first_principles.problem: A single ACL typo during a midnight change window cuts off a data centre for two hours.

analogy.title: Flight simulators for pilots
analogy.story: Instead of testing a manoeuvre in a real plane with passengers, you prove it in a simulator first.
analogy.breaks: Simulators approximate; config verification models can be exact for the logic they cover.

example.title: Before vs after
flow: CI: Batfish proves no reachability loss

check.q: Why are network changes the main source of network outages?
check.a: Manual, unverified edits easily introduce subtle errors whose interactions aren't visible until deployed.

netdevops-applying-software-engineering-.core: NetDevOps treats network configuration as code. A source of truth (NetBox, Nautobot) holds intended state (devices, IPs, VLANs), templates (Jinja2) render device configs, Git and pull requests give review and history, automation (Ansible, Nornir, NAPALM, gNMI) pushes changes, and tests (linting, Batfish, lab emulation) run in CI. Changes become small, reviewed, repeatable and reversible.

first_principles.problem: Switch configs differ subtly across 200 devices because each was hand-edited over years.
derivation: Model intent in a **source of truth**.

analogy.title: A printing press for configs
analogy.story: Instead of hand-copying manuscripts, you typeset once and print identical copies.
analogy.breaks: Printed books don't change; networks need ongoing drift detection.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Dry-run diffs for every leaf before commit.

code.text:
from nornir import InitNornir
from nornir_jinja2.plugins.tasks import template_file
from nornir_napalm.plugins.tasks import napalm_configure

def deploy(task):
    cfg = task.run(template_file, template="leaf.j2", path="templates").result
    task.run(napalm_configure, configuration=cfg, replace=True, dry_run=task.host.get("dry", True))

InitNornir(config_file="nornir.yaml").filter(role="leaf").run(task=deploy)

check.q: What role does a source of truth like NetBox play?
check.a: It holds the intended network state (devices, IPs, VLANs, links) from which configs are generated and against which drift is checked.

config-as-code-vs-intent-based-networkin.core: Config-as-code manages device configurations in Git and templates: you still describe how each device should be configured. Intent-based networking describes what you want (segment A can't reach B, app X needs 10 Gbps), and a system translates that into configs, continuously verifies the network meets it, and alerts or remediates on violation. Most teams combine them: config-as-code for delivery, verification for intent assurance.

first_principles.problem: Configs are in Git, but nobody can prove PCI systems are isolated after each change.
truths: Configs are means, intent is the goal.

analogy.title: Giving directions vs stating the destination
analogy.story: Config-as-code is turn-by-turn directions; intent says 'get me to the airport by 5' and checks you're on track.
analogy.breaks: Satnavs see traffic live; intent systems need good models and telemetry.

example.title: Intent as tests
flow: PCI zone cannot reach corp Wi-Fi
All leaves have 2 uplinks to spines
No device accepts SSH from internet

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Checked on every change and periodically.

check.q: What does intent-based networking add beyond config-as-code?
check.a: Declaring desired outcomes and continuously verifying (and possibly remediating) that the network actually meets them.

formal-verification-the-batfish-model.core: Batfish parses device configs from many vendors into a vendor-neutral model, then simulates the control plane (BGP, OSPF, static routes) to compute each device's forwarding tables and ACL behaviour, without touching the live network. You then query it: 'can host A reach B on 443?', 'which flows does this ACL line affect?', 'are there undefined references?'. It finds errors in planned changes before deployment.

first_principles.problem: A BGP policy change would make a backup link preferred and overload it, which no reviewer noticed.
truths: Queries can cover all flows symbolically.

analogy.title: A wind tunnel for networks
analogy.story: Test the design with simulated airflow and see where it fails, before building the plane.
analogy.breaks: Wind tunnels approximate physics; Batfish can miss bugs in vendor implementations.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: CI fails the PR if the forbidden path exists.

code.text:
from pybatfish.client.session import Session
from pybatfish.datamodel.flow import HeaderConstraints
bf = Session(host="localhost")
bf.init_snapshot("snapshots/proposed", name="proposed", overwrite=True)
ans = bf.q.reachability(
    pathConstraints={"startLocation": "@enter(edge1[Gi0/1])"},
    headers=HeaderConstraints(dstIps="10.50.0.0/24", applications=["ssh"]),
    actions="SUCCESS").answer().frame()
assert ans.empty, "SSH from internet edge reaches PCI subnet!"

check.q: Does Batfish need access to live network devices?
check.a: No, it analyses configuration files (snapshots), simulating the control and data planes offline.

reachability-analysis-proving-the-negati.core: Testing with pings can show that some flows work, but never that no path exists for a forbidden flow. Symbolic reachability analysis (Batfish, AWS Reachability Analyzer and Network Access Analyzer) considers all packets in a header space at once, such as any source IP and any port, and either proves none can reach the target or returns a concrete counterexample flow. That makes isolation claims auditable.

first_principles.problem: An auditor asks for proof that no path exists from the internet to the database subnet, and ping tests can't provide it.
truths: Tests sample; proofs cover all cases.
Header spaces can be reasoned about symbolically.

analogy.title: Proving a maze has no exit vs walking a few paths
analogy.story: Walking some paths and finding no exit proves nothing; mapping the whole maze does.
analogy.breaks: Mazes are static; networks change, so re-verify each change.

code.text:
aws ec2 create-network-insights-access-scope --match-paths '[{"Source":{"ResourceStatement":{"ResourceTypes":["AWS::EC2::InternetGateway"]}},"Destination":{"ResourceStatement":{"Resources":["subnet-0db123"]}}}]'
aws ec2 start-network-insights-access-scope-analysis --network-insights-access-scope-id nis-0abc
# findings: [] → no path from any IGW to DB subnet

check.q: Why can't ping/traceroute tests prove network isolation?
check.a: They only test specific flows; proving no path exists requires reasoning over all possible packets.

differential-analysis-semantic-diffs-for.core: A text diff of configs shows which lines changed, but not what that means for traffic. Differential analysis compares the modelled behaviour of the current and proposed snapshots: which flows newly succeed or fail, which routes change best path, which ACL lines now match different traffic. Reviewers see 'this change blocks HTTPS from branch-12 to CRM', not '+ deny ip any 10.4.0.0 0.0.255.255'.

first_principles.problem: A one-line ACL change looks harmless in the text diff but silently blocks a branch's CRM access.
truths: Behaviour can be compared between snapshots.

analogy.title: Comparing two maps' journey times instead of their ink
analogy.story: Not 'this line moved' but 'trips from A to B now take twice as long'.
analogy.breaks: Maps are visual; behaviour diffs need clear summaries.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reviewer sees the real impact before approving.

code.text:
diff = bf.q.differentialReachability(
    headers=HeaderConstraints(applications=["https"])
).answer(snapshot="proposed", reference_snapshot="current").frame()
print(diff[["Flow", "Snapshot_Traces", "Reference_Traces"]].head())
# Flow: branch-12 → 10.4.2.10:443  current: ACCEPTED  proposed: DENIED

check.q: What does a differential reachability analysis report?
check.a: Flows whose outcome changes between the current and proposed configurations, e.g. newly denied or newly permitted traffic.

the-netdevops-cicd-pipeline-end-to-end.core: A full pipeline runs like this. An engineer updates intent or data in the source of truth or Git; CI renders configs, lints them, loads proposed snapshots into Batfish, runs policy assertions and differential analysis, optionally tests in an emulated lab (Containerlab); a human approves the semantic diff; automation deploys in stages (canary devices first) with automatic rollback on health-check failure; and post-deploy checks and drift detection close the loop.

first_principles.problem: A network team wants software-style confidence for weekly changes across 500 devices.

analogy.title: A car assembly line with quality gates
analogy.story: Every station checks its work, test drives happen before shipping, and recalls are fast.
analogy.breaks: Assembly lines build identical cars; networks are unique topologies.

code.text:
jobs:
  verify:
    steps:
      - run: python render.py --from netbox --out configs/
      - run: batfish-assert --snapshot configs/ --policies policies/
      - run: batfish-diff --base main --proposed configs/ > diff.md
  lab:
    needs: verify
    steps: [ { run: containerlab deploy -t lab.clab.yml && pytest lab_tests/ } ]
  deploy:
    needs: lab
    environment: production   # manual approval
    steps: [ { run: nornir-deploy --canary leaf-01,leaf-02 --then-all --rollback-on-fail } ]

check.q: Why deploy network changes to canary devices first?
check.a: To limit the blast radius and detect real-world problems the models missed before affecting the whole network.
